pages.title: ER diagram | Start with the patient
pages.subtitle: A simplified relationship map. The following pages show all 36 tables in readable sections.
notes: Visits record consultations. Follow-ups record tasks originating from a visit; returning for a consultation creates another visit.
This overview omits staff, identity, audit and questionnaire tables for clarity. They are included on the detailed pages.

pages.title: ER diagram | Staff and audit
pages.subtitle: 7 tables. Role and permission records describe the access model; authentication is not implemented in the current website.
notes: PK = primary key. FK = foreign key. Edge numbers describe how many records can exist at each end.
Example: a role can have many users; a doctor can reference zero or one user, and a user can have at most one doctor profile.

pages.title: ER diagram | Patient identity and safety
pages.subtitle: 7 patient tables, plus referenced doctors and users. The patient-guardian bridge supports many-to-many relationships.
notes: Reference boxes repeat tables owned by another section; they are not extra tables.
Soft-delete columns retain records. The deleted_by relationship points to users; repeated deletion arrows are omitted for readability.

pages.title: ER diagram | Consultations and observations
pages.subtitle: 7 tables, plus referenced patients, doctors and users.
notes: A visit can exist without an appointment. UNIQUE visit_id allows at most one medical record and one growth record per visit.
A visit can have several vital-sign measurements. A medical record can have several diagnoses and treatment records.

pages.title: ER diagram | Prescriptions, labs and follow-ups
pages.subtitle: 8 tables, plus referenced visits, patients, doctors, appointments and users.
notes: Prescription items reference a medication catalogue. Lab orders reference a test catalogue and may have one result.
follow_ups.visit_id points to the originating visit. appointment_id is optional; no completed_visit_id exists in the current schema.

pages.title: ER diagram | Active custom fields
pages.subtitle: 3 tables, plus referenced users. Clinical owners are listed as foreign keys inside the value table.
notes: Active website: clinical_custom_fields -> clinical_custom_field_values -> clinical_custom_field_value_history.
Exactly one of patient, visit, prescription, lab order, allergy, immunization or follow-up owns each value. Owner-table arrows are omitted; the exact foreign keys are listed inside the value table.
CHECK enforces one owner. Triggers ensure the owner matches context_type; the API validates the answer against field_type and validation_rules.

pages.title: ER diagram | JSON questionnaire tables
pages.subtitle: 4 tables, plus referenced visits and users. Database evaluation model; no current questionnaire UI or API.
notes: custom_forms identifies a template version. custom_form_fields holds its questions; answers are stored together in each response JSON object.
UNIQUE (visit_id, form_id) prevents duplicate responses to one template version for one visit. History is linked to the response and revision number.

pages.title: ER diagram | Complete foreign-key map
pages.subtitle: All 36 tables and every declared foreign key, including repeated author/deletion references. Zoom this appendix or open its SVG.
notes: Arrows run from the referenced parent table to the child table carrying the labelled foreign-key column.
1 or 0..1 at the parent end indicates whether the child must reference a parent. 0..N or 0..1 at the child end shows how many children a parent may have.

pages.title: System workflow | Patient care
pages.subtitle: Read from top to bottom. Prescriptions, laboratory work and follow-up tasks are optional branches of a visit.
notes: The repeat-visit loop is a staff workflow; the system does not automatically link a completed follow-up to the later visit.
Appointments and insurance records exist in the database. The current UI does not provide a complete appointment-booking or insurance-editing workflow.

pages.title: System workflow | Customize any clinical form
pages.subtitle: The same dynamic-field component serves patients, visits, prescriptions, labs, allergies, immunizations and follow-ups.
notes: No database column is added when the doctor adds a custom field. A metadata row defines the field, and a value row stores each answer.
The base clinical record and its custom values are saved through separate API calls. The custom-value batch itself uses a transaction.
Retired definitions and their values remain in the database; the active-field UI filters out retired definitions.

pages.title: System workflow | Read, write and preserve data
pages.subtitle: The website uses React, an Express API and MySQL. The diagram shows implemented data paths.
notes: Audit and history links use restrictive retention relationships. Existing data is not physically removed by the clinical soft-delete APIs.
The current prototype uses seeded user_id = 1 for audit actions. Role tables do not yet provide an actual login or enforced authorization flow.

pages.title: EAV explained | Entity + Attribute + Value
pages.subtitle: Illustrative IDs and sample values. EAV is a table design pattern, not a separate database product.
notes: Entity = the clinical record. Attribute = a configurable field. Value = the answer for that field on that record.
The value column above is a classic text-based example; EAV can also use typed columns. Many custom fields mean many value rows and more joins.
Your current website uses this EAV-like relationship pattern with typed JSON in value_json. EAV and JSON can be used together.

pages.title: JSON explained | What the website actually saves
pages.subtitle: The current website stores one typed JSON value for each field and record. It does not put every answer into one response object.
notes: JSON supports strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, objects and null. Dropdown/checkbox options and validation rules also use JSON.
Exactly one owner column is populated: patient_id, visit_id, prescription_id, lab_order_id, allergy_id, immunization_id or follow_up_id.
JSON preserves value types. The API enforces field-specific rules; foreign keys and triggers enforce relationships. Examples above are illustrative, not seeded records.

pages.title: JSON explained | Whole-response document model
pages.subtitle: These questionnaire tables remain in the database for evaluation. Their separate builder page and API have been removed.
notes: Here, all questionnaire answers are keys inside one JSON object. A response is linked to one visit and one template version.
JSON_TYPE checks the document shape; it does not enforce each field definition or make a template immutable. Those rules need a controlled write path.
Compare: active website = one JSON value per field; questionnaire model = one JSON object per form response. Both retain relational foreign keys.
